attributes.description:
Overview

This feature service provides comprehensive tax-related business information for local businesses within Broward County as well as businesses located outside Broward County. It consolidates data from two primary feature layers that represent business tax databases, supporting up-to-date business tax tracking and management.

Feature Layers
  • Local Business Tax Database: This layer contains detailed business tax records for local Broward County businesses, including business names, owner information, addresses, and tax payment details. The dataset features historical and current tax data updated as of late 2024, providing valuable insights into business activities, tax categories, and business start dates within the county.
  • Non-Broward Business Address: Complementing the local layer, this layer holds tax and address information for businesses located outside Broward County but relevant for tax tracking purposes. Updated through 2022, it maintains consistent fields with the local layer, allowing for comprehensive tax record management across regions.
Geographic Coverage

The service centers on Broward County, Florida, with the primary focus on local businesses within the county limits and an additional scope covering businesses from outside the county, providing an inclusive regional tax database.

Use Cases
  • Support for local government agencies in tax collection, auditing, and compliance monitoring.
  • Business analytics and economic development planning using detailed business tax and category data.
  • Facilitating public and administrative access to updated tax records and business information by geographic location and tax year.

attributes.description:
Business Improvement Districts (BID). The dataset contains locations and attributes of the BID jurisdictions (Downtown, Golden Triangle, Mt. Vernon Triangle, Adams Morgan, Georgetown, and NoMa), first authorized under the Business Improvement Districts Act of 1996. This layer also contains the Mt. Vernon Community Improvement District (CID). Jurisdictions were identified from public records (websites, legacy GIS data, real property records).

A Business Improvement District (BID) is a self-taxing district established by property owners to enhance the economic vitality of a specific commercial area. The tax is a surcharge on the real property tax liability. The tax is collected by the District of Columbia and all revenues are returned entirely to the nonprofit organization managing the BID. Business and property owners control the BID and how funds are spent. There are currently 12 BIDs in the District of Columbia.

The Department of Small and Local Business Development manages the certification of BIDs and the BID charter extension process.

prcStep.stepDesc: Capitol Hill BID development: The DC Office of Planning created the Capitol Hill Business Improvement District (CHBID) by head's up digitizing the BID boundaries. This boundary is based on the legislation, DC Code ? 2-1215.04, the Establishment of Business Improvement District. OCTO GIS base map planimetrics were used as a guide, but the linework is not snapped to the snapbase. OCTO GIS staff populated appropriate attribution for consistency. Note that there is an overlap between the Downtown BID and Capitol Hill BID.

OCTO GIS staff generated the boundary for the Mount Vernon CID based off of text description in 'The Brazil Bulletin'. OCTO GIS base map planimetrics were used as a guide, but the linework is not snapped to the snapbase. Instead, it is snapped along key common points. Then staff populated the appropriate attribution for consistency in the BID layer.

Staff created the NoMa BID boundaries based on a description and consultation with Barry Margeson, from the DC Executive Office of mayor. Using street centerlines, planimetric buildings, and the 2005 orthophoto, staff digitized the boundaries for the BID.

Staff created the Adams Morgan BID boundaries based on a source map and the legislation provided by Josh Gibson of the Adams Morgan Partnership. Using street centerlines, vector property lines (record and tax lots), and planimetric buildings, staff digitized the boundaries for the BID.
Merged the two Downtown BID polygons into one polygon. There should only be one Downtown BID polygon, per their website, www.downtowndc.org

Jurisdictions were identified from public records (the three individual websites, legacy GIS data, real property records) and heads-up digitized from the 1995 orthophotographs. Downtown DC BID provided information for Golden Triangle BID. A base ArcInfo coverage of correct line work (snapbase.e00) for all DC data was developed after the final delivery of the planimetric street centerlines. The datasets were selected from the snapbase coverage, creating coincident geography with the other DC GIS datasets. When imported into the DC GIS geodatabase the coverages shift 0.01mm since the geodatabase supports only 11 digits of precision, not double precision (16 digits). An initial shapefile for each BID was compared to the snapbase linework and a coverage of the correct linework selected out, creating a topologically correct feature. This was built into a polygon. Georgetown Partnership BID was created by selecting non-residentially zoned real property owner points to start. Residentially zoned properties are not included in the Georgetown BID. The properties corresponding to these were outlined. This leaves an irregular coverage with holes for those excepted properties. Attribute data was provided by public records and verified against the BID websites and personal interview. Planimetrics were created at a scale of 1:1,000. This means that a well defined feature falls within two feet of true position. All DC GIS data is stored and exported in Maryland State Plane coordinates NAD 83 meters.

dataIdInfo.suppInfo: Establishment of BIDs in Washington has been a top economic development priority for the city and private sector since 1996 when the Council, Mayor and business community worked together to pass the Business Improvement Districts Act of 1996. http://www.downtowndc.org/About/bid.html DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA OFFICIAL CODE 2001 EDITION DIVISION I. GOVERNMENT OF DISTRICT. TITLE 2. GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATION. CHAPTER 12. BUSINESS AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT. SUBCHAPTER VIII. BUSINESS IMPROVEMENT DISTRICTS. Law 11-134, the "Business Improvement Districts Act of 1996," was introduced in Council and Assigned Bill No. 11-464, which was referred to the Committee on Economic Development. The Bill was adopted on first and second readings on February 6, 1996, and March 5, 1996, respectively. Signed by the Mayor on March 25, 1996, it was assigned Act No. 11-242 and transmitted to both Houses of Congress for its review. D.C. Law 11-134 became effective on May 29, 1996. Law 12-23, the "Business Improvement Districts Temporary Amendment Act of 1997," was introduced in Council and assigned Bill No. 12-230. The Bill was adopted on first and second readings on May 20, 1997, and June 3, 1997, respectively. Signed by the Mayor on June 18, 1997, it was assigned Act No. 12-100 and transmitted to both Houses of Congress for its review. D.C. Law 12- 23 became effective on September 23, 1997. Law 12-26, the "Business Improvement Districts Amendment Act of 1997," was introduced in Council and assigned Bill No. 12-225, which was referred to the Committee on Economic Development. The Bill was adopted on first and second readings on June 3, 1997, and June 17, 1997, respectively. Signed by the Mayor on July 3, 1997, it was assigned Act No. 12-109 and transmitted to both Houses of Congress for its review. D.C. Law 12-26 became effective on October 8, 1997.

attributes.description:
Overview

This feature service presents parcel-based business and tax records for Broward County, Florida. It brings together property, business, ownership, contact, assessment, and district information to support county operations, commercial property review, and local administrative analysis.

Feature Layers
  • BrowardBiz_TaxRoll — A countywide parcel layer with business and tax roll information tied to individual properties. It includes business and owner names, site and mailing addresses, parcel and legal reference details, use and classification information, property value and exemption data, taxable amounts, assessment-related fields, district and service area attributes, structure characteristics, and business registration details such as account, receipt, and status information.
Geographic Coverage

The service covers Broward County, Florida and provides a parcel-level view of business-related property records across the county.

Use Cases
  • Business parcel and commercial property review
  • Tax assessment and account tracking
  • Ownership and contact record lookup
  • Economic development and local business analysis
  • County administrative and property record management

attributes.description:
Overview

This feature service provides detailed information on local businesses registered for tax purposes within Broward County, Florida. It includes comprehensive data concerning business names, ownership, addresses, and contact details, such as phone numbers and email addresses. The spatial data is referenced in a local coordinate system and covers a geographic area within Broward County.

Feature Layer
  • LocalTaxBusinessesEmailPhone: This layer captures extensive business tax registration data, including business and DBA names, owner details, business and mailing addresses, and related contact information like business and owner emails and phone numbers. The layer also contains fields related to business start and close dates, account status and balances, and classification descriptors which provide context for business categorization. It integrates administrative and postal data, supporting multiple district and perimeter classifications relevant to local governance and tax authorities.
Geographic Coverage

The data focuses on Broward County, Florida, highlighting economic activities within the county through the tax registrations of local businesses. It includes address information within city limits and postal codes relevant to the area.

Use Cases
  • Enabling local governments and tax authorities to manage and monitor business tax compliance.
  • Supporting economic development analyses by providing a detailed snapshot of local business operations and classifications.
  • Assisting public and private sector stakeholders in identifying and contacting local businesses for outreach, marketing, or community engagement purposes.
